traveler: Leif Erikson (Leifr Eiriksson, Leif the Lucky)
title: The Booths at the River Mouth: Greenland, Vinland, and the Winter Without Frost
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Outlawries of Erik the Red

stops.name: Drangar, Hornstrandir: the family arrives outlawed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Landnamabok and Eiriks saga rauda ch. 1 name Drangar as Thorvald Asvaldsson's settlement after a killing in Norway, but give no year; the date here is a placeholder for Erik's boyhood.
stops.campa: Thorvald Asvaldsson kills a man in Jaeren and takes his household west to Iceland, where the good land is already taken. What is left for him is Drangar on the Hornstrandir, the northernmost coast, cliff and drift ice and a short summer. His son Erik grows up there. The pattern is set two generations before Leif is born: a killing, a sentence, a sail into colder water, a farm at the edge of what a family can hold. Leif's grandfather never sees the green south of Iceland. His grandson will not see Iceland at all after infancy.
suggested_refs: The Hornstrandir cliffs at Drangar, northernmost settled coast of Iceland
sources: Saga of Erik the Red (Eiriks saga rauda), ch. 1

stops.name: Eiriksstadir, Haukadalur: the birth no saga records
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no saga states where or when Leif was born. The year c. 970 is a scholarly estimate; Eiriksstadir is tradition, carried by the reconstructed farm on the site, and Breidafjordur generally is the most that can be defended.
stops.campa: Erik the Red marries Thjodhild and builds Eiriksstadir in the Haukadalur valley, in the soft green country behind Breidafjordur that comes to him through his wife's family. A son is born and named Leif. No saga says so. No saga gives the year, the month, or the house. Iceland simply produces him, the way it produces the men in the law-cases around him, and the written record picks him up thirty years later fully grown, standing in a Norwegian hall. The turf walls at Eiriksstadir are rebuilt for visitors now on the strength of the tradition.
stops.quote: Leif was a big, strong man, the handsomest of men in appearance, and clever; in fact he was in all respects an excellent commander.
stops.quote_source: The Norse Discoverers of America: The Wineland Sagas, tr. G. M. Gathorne-Hardy (1921), Project Gutenberg #76383
suggested_refs: The reconstructed longhouse at Eiriksstadir, Haukadalur, built on the traditional site
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 2

stops.name: Thorsnes: the assembly that sentences a family westward
stops.date_confidence: attested in Eiriks saga rauda ch. 2 for the outlawry and its three-year term. Coordinate corrected: the Thorsnes thing site lies on the north coast of Snaefellsnes near Helgafell and Stykkisholmur, not on the south coast.
stops.campa: Erik kills Eyjolf Saur and Hrafn the Dueller in a quarrel over borrowed bench-boards, and then kills the sons of Thorgest at Oxney over the boards again. The assembly at Thorsnes hears the case and sentences him to three years out of the country. Icelandic law does not hang men. It removes them and lets distance do what a gallows would do elsewhere. The sentence is meant to be temporary and reversible. What it produces is Greenland, and Greenland produces the westernmost voyage anyone in the Norse world will make.
suggested_refs: The Thorsnes thing site under Helgafell, Snaefellsnes
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 2

stops.name: Ondverdarnes: the sail set into the unknown west
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the saga has Erik put out from under Snaefellsjokull; the precise departure point is inferred, and the month is not given.
stops.campa: From the tip of Snaefellsnes, under the glacier, Erik puts out west with what he has. He is following a rumour: land sighted by Gunnbjorn Ulfsson generations back and never landed on. He spends the three years of his sentence coasting fjords nobody has named, and names them, one of them after himself. Leif is an infant in Iceland or not yet born. His father is at this moment inventing the country the boy will be raised in, on the strength of a sentence handed down by neighbours who wanted him gone.
suggested_refs: Ondverdarnes and the Snaefellsjokull headland, departure coast for the Greenland voyages
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 2

segments.name: Greenland, a Country Named to Attract Settlers

stops.name: Eiriksfjord: three years of exile spent surveying
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exile and the naming (Eiriks saga rauda ch. 2, Groenlendinga saga); the day and month are conventional, the span 982 to 985 is the saga's own three-year term.
stops.campa: Erik winters three times in the fjord he names for himself and finds it will carry cattle, sheep, and hay through a Greenland summer. In 985 he sails back to Breidafjordur and tells Iceland what is out there. He calls the country Greenland, the saga says, because men will be much readier to go if the land has a good name. Twenty-five ships leave the following spring. Fourteen arrive. The rest turn back or are lost, and the colony Leif will inherit begins with a name chosen to recruit.
suggested_refs: Tunulliarfik Fjord, the Eiriksfjord of the sagas
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 2

stops.name: Brattahlid: the farm at the head of the fjord
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding (Groenlendinga saga; Saga of Erik the Red) and confirmed archaeologically at Qassiarsuk. Coordinate corrected to 61.150 / -45.517, the Qassiarsuk site; a widely circulated 61.1667 / -45.4167 sits several kilometres northeast of the ruins.
stops.campa: At the head of Eiriksfjord, on the one broad shelf of grass in a country of rock, Erik takes the best site for himself and calls it Brattahlid, the steep slope. There is no king in Greenland and no lord set over him. He holds the country by having found it, and the men who came out on his word farm the fjords below him. Leif is a small child when the household is unloaded. He will live at Brattahlid the rest of his life, sail from it twice, and die in it, and the ruins at Qassiarsuk are still being dug.
suggested_refs: The excavated farm complex at Qassiarsuk, Greenland, identified as Brattahlid

stops.name: Herjolfsnes: Bjarni brings back a coastline he did not land on
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 2-3; absent entirely from the Saga of Erik the Red, which knows no Bjarni Herjolfsson. Coordinate corrected to 59.983 / -44.700 (Ikigaat).
stops.campa: Herjolf Bardsson sails in Erik's fleet and takes the southern promontory, the first landfall for any ship coming from Iceland. His son Bjarni, arriving a season late, is blown past Greenland entirely and raises three unknown coasts in succession: wooded and low, then flat and wooded, then high and glaciered. He does not go ashore. He is looking for his father, not for a country. He corrects course, finds Herjolfsnes, and tells the story at his father's table, where it sits for fifteen years until someone at Brattahlid decides it is worth a ship.
suggested_refs: Ikigaat, the Herjolfsnes of the sagas, principal port of call of the Eastern Settlement

stops.name: Brattahlid: Tyrker the thrall is given the boy to raise
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga only, and undated there; the year is a placeholder for Leif's childhood. Widely miscited to the Saga of Erik the Red, which does not contain Tyrker at all.
stops.campa: Erik gives the boy into the keeping of Tyrker, a thrall of his household, a southerner the saga calls German, small and slight, with a jutting forehead and restless eyes. Fosterage in this society is a real bond and sometimes a stronger one than blood. Tyrker raises him and Leif calls him fostri. But Tyrker appears in only one of the two sagas: Groenlendinga saga has him throughout, and Eiriks saga rauda does not know he exists. The man closest to Leif in childhood is, by half the record, not there at all.
suggested_refs: Groenlendinga saga's Tyrker, the one named foster-father in the Vinland corpus

stops.name: Nidaros: Leif enters the king's hird
stops.date_confidence: attested in both sagas (Groenlendinga saga ch. 5; Saga of Erik the Red ch. 5) for the visit and the retainership; the year 999 is the conventional dating, constrained by Olaf Tryggvason's reign of 995 to 1000.
stops.campa: Leif takes ship for Norway, the country his grandfather was driven out of, and presents himself at Nidaros, the town Olaf Tryggvason has founded as his seat. The king takes him into the hird. Every chieftain's son from Iceland and Greenland who matters does this; it is how a man from the edge acquires standing at the centre. Njal's people make the same crossing to the same court, and Flosi will stand in this hall a decade after Leif leaves it. The hird takes in men from the whole northern rim and keeps them through the winter.
stops.quote: It is my purpose, if it be your will.
stops.quote_source: The Saga of Eric the Red, tr. Julius E. Olson, Original Narratives of Early American History, Project Gutenberg #18571
suggested_refs: Olaf Tryggvason's royal seat at Nidaros, founded c. 997
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 5

stops.name: Nidaros: baptism, and an errand for Greenland
stops.date_confidence: attested in both sagas for the baptism and the commission. Dated here to 999 or the winter of 999-1000: Olaf Tryggvason died at Svolder on 9 September 1000, so a flat date of 1000 risks placing the commission after the king's death.
stops.campa: Olaf Tryggvason is converting Norway with the same energy he brings to everything else, and he converts his Greenlander. Leif is baptized at court, and the king hands him the errand: take priests home, bring the new faith to the settlements. Leif answers, in reported speech rather than in his own voice, that the king should decide but that the work will be difficult in Greenland. He asks for one thing, the king's protection, and goes. In the same season Iceland's Althing votes Christianity into law under pressure from the same king.
stops.quote: Thou shalt go my errand, and preach Christianity in Greenland.
stops.quote_source: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. J. Sephton (1880), sagadb.org
suggested_refs: The Althing's conversion vote of 999/1000, driven by the same king; see burnt_njal
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 5
Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. Sephton (1880)

stops.name: The Hebrides: Thorgunna, and a son Leif does not take home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the episode is in the Saga of Erik the Red ch. 5 alone and is absent from Groenlendinga saga; the text names no island, so the coordinate marks the Outer Hebrides generally. Eyrbyggja saga knows a Thorgils Leifsson independently.
stops.campa: Sailing home, Leif is held in the Hebrides by contrary winds through most of a summer. There he takes up with a woman of rank named Thorgunna, who asks to sail with him and is refused; he will not carry a foreign noblewoman into his father's house. She tells him she is carrying his son and that the boy will come to Greenland one day. He does. Thorgils Leifsson turns up years later and is not much liked. Only Eiriks saga rauda tells any of this. The other saga sends Leif straight home.
suggested_refs: Thorgils Leifsson in Eyrbyggja saga, the only external trace of the Hebridean son
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 5

segments.name: The Two Accounts of How Vinland Was Found

stops.name: The North Atlantic: where the sagas part company
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: this stop marks a contradiction, not a place. The coordinate is a mid-passage marker between Norway and Greenland and corresponds to no event either saga locates.
stops.campa: Here the record forks and does not rejoin. Eiriks saga rauda has Leif driven off course between Norway and Greenland, coming upon lands he never looked for, gathering grapes and self-sown wheat from a coast he cannot place, and reaching home by luck. Groenlendinga saga has none of it: Leif sails home cleanly, hears Bjarni's story, buys Bjarni's ship, and goes west on purpose fifteen years later. Accident, or intention. Both sagas are Icelandic, both are canonical, and neither one yields.
suggested_refs: The unreconciled discovery accounts of the two Vinland sagas

stops.name: Brattahlid: the ship bought, and the horse that falls
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga for the purchase, the crew of thirty-five, and Erik's fall; the whole episode is absent from the Saga of Erik the Red, which has no deliberate expedition to describe.
stops.campa: Leif buys Bjarni Herjolfsson's ship, the one that has already been where he means to go, and finds thirty-five men to sail it. He asks his father to lead them. Erik says he is too old, then agrees. Riding down to the shore he is thrown from his horse and hurts his foot, and he turns back, saying he is not meant to find any more countries than the one he lives in. It is the last thing the old man does in the story. His son sails without him, west and north, into weather nobody has charted.
suggested_refs: Bjarni Herjolfsson's ship, the only vessel in the corpus with a prior sighting to its name

stops.name: Helluland: the land of flat stones
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the landfall and the naming are attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 5, but the identification with Baffin Island is scholarly consensus rather than textual fact, and the coordinate is approximate at the scale of a whole coast.
stops.campa: The first land they raise has no grass on it. From the sea to the glaciers behind, it is one slab of flat rock, and Leif goes ashore only long enough to say that they have at least set foot on it, unlike Bjarni. He names it Helluland, the land of flat stones, and puts back out. Scholars read it as Baffin Island and cannot prove it. Everything named on this voyage is named the same way: the land is called what it looks like, and no saint and no king gets a coastline out of it.
suggested_refs: The Baffin Island coast, standard modern identification of Helluland

stops.name: Markland: the land of forests
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: naming attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 5; the traditional identification with the Labrador coast near Cape Porcupine is inference, and the exact landfall is unknown.
stops.campa: The second land is low and wooded to the waterline, with white sand shelving into the sea, and the crew go ashore among the trees. Leif names it Markland, forest land, and does not stay. Greenland has no timber. Every plank in the colony has come from Norway or off the beach as driftwood, and a coast of standing trees two days' sail from home is worth more to a Greenland chieftain than any weight of silver. The Icelandic annals will still be recording voyages to Markland for wood three centuries later.
suggested_refs: The Labrador coast near Cape Porcupine, traditional Markland

stops.name: Furdustrandir: the wonder strands
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a flagged cross-saga contradiction: the name is given in the Saga of Erik the Red ch. 8, where it belongs to Karlsefni's later voyage retracing this route. Groenlendinga saga does not use the word for Leif's voyage at all.
stops.campa: South of Markland the shore runs on and on, one unbroken beach without a headland or a river mouth, and the crews take so long passing it that they call it Furdustrandir, the wonder strands. Which of the two crews names it is unsettled. Eiriks saga rauda gives the name to Karlsefni's expedition years afterwards; Groenlendinga saga never applies it to Leif. The beach itself is real, and Labrador has one, sixty kilometres of it. Whose ship first counted it out is a matter between two manuscripts.
suggested_refs: The long sand beaches of southern Labrador, candidate Furdustrandir
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 8

stops.name: L'Anse aux Meadows: the booths built and the salmon counted
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 5 for the camp, the river, the lake, and the salmon; the identification of Leifsbudir with the excavated Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows is scholarly inference and is not textually proven.
stops.campa: They pass an island, then a cape, and run into a sound between the island and the mainland, and where a river comes out of a lake into the sea they carry their gear ashore. Leif orders houses built, big ones, not booths for a single season. The river is full of salmon larger than any of them have seen and the men take them without difficulty. There is grass to the water's edge. He calls the place Leifsbudir, Leif's booths, and it is the first building the Norse are known to have put up in North America.
suggested_refs: The eight excavated turf structures at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland

stops.name: Leifsbudir: Tyrker comes back speaking German
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 5 and in Gathorne-Hardy's translation of it; entirely absent from the Saga of Erik the Red, along with Tyrker himself.
stops.campa: Leif divides the company: half explore each day, half stay at the houses, and nobody goes further than can be walked back before dark. One evening Tyrker is missing. Leif goes out after his foster-father angry and frightened, and meets him coming back rolling his eyes and grinning, talking German for a long while before anyone can get sense out of him. He has found vines and grapes. He says he knows them because he was born where there was no lack of either. Leif names the whole country after them.
stops.quote: I did not go much further than you, (but) I have found something fresh to report. I found vines and grapes.
stops.quote_source: The Norse Discoverers of America: The Wineland Sagas, tr. G. M. Gathorne-Hardy (1921), Project Gutenberg #76383
suggested_refs: Gathorne-Hardy's 1921 translation of the Wineland sagas
sources: Gathorne-Hardy, The Norse Discoverers of America (1921)

stops.name: The Gulf of St Lawrence: the grape country the site cannot supply
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no saga names this coast and no Norse structure has been found on it. The pin is placed on the botanical argument alone, from the northern range of wild grape and butternut, and marks a place the sagas locate at the door of Leifsbudir.
stops.campa: The vines are a problem. Wild grapes do not grow at the latitude of L'Anse aux Meadows and have not in the Holocene; the northern limit lies hundreds of kilometres southwest, around the Gulf of St Lawrence. But butternuts were dug at the Newfoundland site, along with wood worked from a butternut tree, and butternuts grow in exactly the country the grapes grow in. Somebody from that camp sailed southwest and came back with the fruit of a warmer coast. The saga puts the vines outside the door.
stops.quote: There were fields of wild wheat, and the vine-tree in full growth.
stops.quote_source: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. J. Sephton (1880), sagadb.org
suggested_refs: The butternuts and butternut-worked wood excavated at L'Anse aux Meadows, outside the site's own botanical range
sources: Wikipedia, 'L'Anse aux Meadows' (butternut evidence and the grape problem)

stops.name: Leifsbudir: the winter in which the grass does not wither
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 5 as the saga's own description, not as a climatic fact; the common paraphrase that no snow fell is an embellishment the text does not contain.
stops.campa: They winter over. No frost comes, the saga says; the grass hardly withers and the cattle need neither fodder nor a byre. Day and night are more evenly divided than in Greenland or Iceland, and on the shortest day of the year the sun is still up in the middle of the afternoon. Whatever coast this describes, it is not one a Greenlander could have invented from his own weather. Later readers turn the passage into a country where no snow falls. The saga does not say that. It says the grass stays green.
stops.quote: There were self-sown wheat fields and vines growing there.
stops.quote_source: The Saga of Eric the Red, tr. Julius E. Olson, Original Narratives of Early American History, Project Gutenberg #18571
suggested_refs: The saga's daylight observation, sometimes used to estimate the latitude of Vinland
sources: Saga of Eric the Red, tr. Olson

stops.name: Leifsbudir: grapes and timber loaded for home
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga for the cargo and the division of labour; the month is the saga's spring, not a recorded date.
stops.campa: In spring Leif splits the work and keeps the days separate: one day the men gather grapes and cut vines, the next they fell wood, until the ship is loaded to the gunwales and the tow-boat behind her is filled with fruit. He leaves nobody behind to hold the ground. The cargo is what he wants out of Vinland: it proves the country and pays for the ship, and the country will keep until somebody else comes for it. The houses stand empty behind them. They will be used three more times and never once by Leif.
stops.quote: We will now do two things, keeping separate days for each; we will gather grapes and cut down vines, and fell wood, to make a cargo for my ship.
stops.quote_source: The Norse Discoverers of America: The Wineland Sagas, tr. G. M. Gathorne-Hardy (1921), Project Gutenberg #76383
suggested_refs: The Vinland timber trade, the colony's only source of building wood
sources: Gathorne-Hardy, The Norse Discoverers of America (1921)

stops.name: The skerry: fifteen people taken off a wreck
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga, which names Thorir the Norwegian merchant and his wife Gudrid. The Saga of Erik the Red does not mention Thorir at all, and the two sources place the byname's origin differently; the position at sea is approximate and disputed between an Atlantic and a near-Greenland location.
stops.campa: On the crossing home, running with a fair wind, Leif sees something on a skerry that turns out to be men. Fifteen of them are alive on the rock: a Norwegian merchant named Thorir, his wife Gudrid, and their crew, wrecked and waiting. He takes them all off, gives them passage, and finds them winter quarters at Brattahlid, where Thorir dies of sickness before spring. Gudrid does not. She will marry two more men in this story and outlive the whole Vinland enterprise, one wreck and three husbands later.
stops.quote: Leif found men upon a wreck, and took them home with him, and procured quarters for them all during the winter. In this wise he showed his nobleness and goodness, since he introduced Christianity into the country, and saved the men from the wreck; and he was called Leif the Lucky ever after.
stops.quote_source: The Saga of Eric the Red, tr. Julius E. Olson, Original Narratives of Early American History, Project Gutenberg #18571
suggested_refs: Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir, the one person present at nearly every Vinland voyage
sources: Saga of Eric the Red, tr. Olson

stops.name: Brattahlid: the cargo landed and the name earned
stops.date_confidence: attested in both sagas for the return, the cargo, and the byname heppni; the sagas disagree on which act earns it, the rescue or the Christian mission, and Sephton's translation gives it flatly with no reason attached.
stops.campa: The ship comes into Eiriksfjord loaded with timber and dried grapes and carrying fifteen people who should be dead. Greenland gives him the name on the strength of the rescue and the cargo together: Leif heppni, Leif the Lucky, the man whose voyages come out right. He is about thirty. He has crossed to a continent, wintered on it, named it, and brought back proof, and the whole of it took one summer, one winter, and one spring. There is a country to the west now, and every table in the Eastern Settlement knows its name.
stops.quote: He was called Leif the Lucky.
stops.quote_source: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. J. Sephton (1880), sagadb.org
suggested_refs: The byname heppni, the Norse epithet for a man whose luck holds
sources: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. Sephton (1880)

stops.name: Brattahlid: Thjodhild builds a church her husband will not enter
stops.date_confidence: attested in both sagas for the mission and Thjodhild's church, and confirmed by the excavated church ruin at Qassiarsuk; the year is conventional. The ruin lies a few hundred metres from the farm mound, inside the same site, not in a separate coordinate cluster.
stops.campa: Leif lands the priests too, and the king's errand goes to work. He preaches the new faith through the settlements and his mother takes it. Thjodhild builds a church a little way from the farmhouse, small, turf-walled, room for perhaps thirty people standing, and refuses her husband her bed until he is baptized. Erik the Red is not baptized. He keeps to Thor and dies keeping to him. The ruin was dug at Qassiarsuk in the 1960s, with a churchyard around it holding both sexes and all ages.
stops.quote: He soon after preached Christianity and catholic truth throughout the land, making known to the people the message of King Olaf Tryggvason.
stops.quote_source: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. J. Sephton (1880), sagadb.org
suggested_refs: Thjodhild's church ruin and churchyard at Qassiarsuk, Greenland's first Christian building
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 5
Excavation of the Qassiarsuk church ruin

stops.name: Brattahlid: Erik the Red dies and the chieftaincy passes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: both sagas place Erik's death not long after 1000 and neither gives a year; 1003 is a conventional estimate. The succession of Leif to the chieftaincy is attested, the date is not.
stops.campa: Erik the Red dies at Brattahlid not long after his son comes home, and the sagas give him no death scene worth the name. Leif takes the farm and the chieftaincy of the Eastern Settlement, and from that day he never sails west again. The man who found Vinland spends the rest of his recorded life administering a colony of a few hundred households on the near side of the Davis Strait, lending out his ship and his houses to brothers and in-laws who go where he went and come back worse off.
suggested_refs: The chieftaincy of the Eastern Settlement, Greenland's only paramount authority before the bishopric

stops.name: Krossanes: Thorvald is buried under two crosses
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the episode is attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 7, but Krossanes has never been located and the coordinate is a placeholder in the Leifsbudir region. The year is conventional.
stops.campa: Thorvald Eriksson borrows his brother's ship and his brother's houses and takes thirty men west. He explores two summers out of Leifsbudir, finds a headland he likes well enough to say he would settle there, and takes an arrow under the arm when nine men in skin boats fight back after his crew have killed eight of them asleep. He tells them to bury him on the headland with a cross at his head and a cross at his feet, and to call the place Krossanes. He is the first Norseman to die in America.
suggested_refs: Krossanes, the unlocated headland of the first Norse burial in North America

stops.name: Leifsbudir: Karlsefni borrows the houses, or does not
stops.date_confidence: attested in both sagas that Karlsefni led the largest expedition, and flagged as a contradiction on where he based it: Groenlendinga saga has him at Leif's houses at Leifsbudir, while the Saga of Erik the Red has him found his own camp at Straumfjord and never mentions Leifsbudir. Karlsefni was not Leif's brother-in-law; his only tie is his marriage to Gudrid.
stops.campa: Thorfinn Karlsefni, a rich Icelandic trader with no kinship to Leif, marries the widow Gudrid and takes a real colonizing party west: sixty men, five women, livestock. Where he bases them depends on which saga is open. Groenlendinga saga has him borrow Leif's houses at Leifsbudir, which Leif lends and will not sell. Eiriks saga rauda has him found his own camp at Straumfjord and never mentions Leif's houses at all. Gudrid bears a son called Snorri, the first European child born in the Americas.
suggested_refs: Snorri Thorfinnsson, born in Vinland, ancestor of a line of Icelandic bishops
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 8-13

stops.name: Hop: the tidal lagoon and the end of the settlement
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Hop appears in the Saga of Erik the Red ch. 11-12 only and is absent from Groenlendinga saga. The place has never been securely identified and the coordinate is a guess along a plausible southern coast.
stops.campa: Karlsefni's people move south to a tidal lagoon they call Hop, where a river runs out of a lake and the tide strands their ship on the flats twice a day. There is self-sown wheat on the low ground and vines on the slopes. Skraelings come to trade furs for milk and red cloth, then come back armed, and the settlement that was supposed to hold a country is given up after three winters. Hop has never been found. One saga tells the whole of it and the other has never heard the name.
suggested_refs: Hop, the southern camp of the Saga of Erik the Red, unlocated
sources: Saga of Erik the Red, ch. 11-12

stops.name: Leifsbudir: Freydis and the two ships
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 9, and absent from the Saga of Erik the Red, which has no massacre. Kinship contradiction flagged: the saga that tells this story calls Freydis Leif's full sister, while the Saga of Erik the Red makes her Erik's illegitimate daughter and so a half-sister.
stops.campa: Freydis Eiriksdottir goes west with two Icelandic brothers, Helgi and Finnbogi, in two ships, having agreed on equal numbers of men and then smuggled five extra aboard her own. She borrows Leif's houses as the others have done and takes them for herself when the brothers arrive. Over a winter of quarrels she provokes her husband into killing the brothers and all their men, and when nobody will kill the five women she takes an axe and does it herself. Then she loads the better ship and sails home.
suggested_refs: Groenlendinga saga ch. 9, the only account of the Vinland massacre

stops.name: Brattahlid: Leif does not punish his sister
stops.date_confidence: attested in Groenlendinga saga ch. 9; undated in the text, and the year follows from the narrative sequence rather than from any record.
stops.campa: The ship comes back loaded and Freydis pays her crew to say nothing. Word gets out anyway. Leif has three of her people seized and tortured until the accounts match, and then does nothing: he says he has not the heart to treat his sister as she deserves, but that he predicts poor luck for her line. The saga notes that he is right, in that nobody thinks well of them afterwards. It is the last act of Leif Erikson in the Vinland story. The massacre is proved to a chieftain's satisfaction and no sentence follows.
suggested_refs: The Greenland chieftaincy's want of any court above the household

stops.name: The Western Settlement: the outer bound of a chieftaincy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weakly attested at that: no saga sends Leif to the Western Settlement, and the connection is inferred from Groenlendinga saga's picture of how the colony was organized. The date is arbitrary within his chieftaincy.
stops.campa: Four hundred sea-miles up the coast from Brattahlid lies the other Norse colony, the Western Settlement, ninety farms in the fjords behind what is now Nuuk. As paramount chief of the Eastern Settlement Leif is the nearest thing Greenland has to a head, and tradition puts the western farms somewhere within his reach. No saga sends him there. It is the outer bound of a jurisdiction nobody described, over perhaps three thousand people strung along two strips of habitable fjord.
suggested_refs: The Western Settlement in the fjords behind Nuuk, abandoned in the fourteenth century

stops.name: Brattahlid: the last mention of a living man
stops.date_confidence: attested as a passing reference in the Saga of Saint Olaf within the Heimskringla tradition, which places Leif alive and chief in Greenland; the year is conventional and the notice carries no date of its own.
stops.campa: The Saga of Saint Olaf notes in passing that Leif Erikson is in Greenland, alive and chief there. That is all of it. He is about fifty. Then the record stops attending to him mid-sentence, the way it stops attending to any man in Greenland once the story goes back to Norway. He was baptized by one Norwegian king and ends as a clause in the saga of the next. The colony he governs will last four hundred years more and never produce another name anyone remembers.
suggested_refs: The Saga of Saint Olaf, last text to place Leif Erikson among the living

stops.name: Brattahlid: a death no saga records
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and an honest gap: no saga records the year, manner, or place of Leif's death, or names a grave. The bound comes from his son Thorkell Leifsson holding the chieftaincy by 1025; scholars place the death between 1018 and 1025.
stops.campa: No saga records the death of Leif Erikson: not the year, not the manner, not the place, not a grave. By 1025 his son Thorkell Leifsson holds the chieftaincy, which means the father is dead. Scholars put it between 1018 and 1025 and name Brattahlid as the presumed place, because there is nowhere else it would have happened. The man who supplies a hemisphere with a discovery date has no death date of his own, and the ground at Qassiarsuk has yielded no bone anyone can attach to him.
suggested_refs: Thorkell Leifsson, attested holding the Greenland chieftaincy by 1025
sources: Saga of Erik the Red (Thorkell's tenure)

stops.name: Gardar: a bishop's seat, a hundred and twenty years late
stops.date_confidence: attested for the bishopric: Sokki Thorisson petitioned King Sigurd I, Arnaldur was ordained in 1124 and arrived in 1126. The traditional line from Leif's mission to Gardar is reconstruction only, and it skips roughly one hundred and twenty-five years.
stops.campa: Across the fjord from Brattahlid, at Igaliku, the Greenlanders raise a cathedral of red sandstone with a bell tower and a byre big enough for a hundred cattle, and Greenland gets a bishop of its own. This happens in the 1120s and not in Leif's lifetime: Sokki Thorisson petitions the king of Norway, Arnaldur is ordained in 1124 and lands in 1126. The line drawn from Leif's imported priests to Gardar's seat skips five generations. Tradition draws it anyway, because the errand from Nidaros wants a destination.
suggested_refs: The cathedral ruins at Igaliku, seat of the bishops of Gardar

stops.name: Iceland: two sagas written down two centuries later
stops.date_confidence: attested that both Vinland sagas are thirteenth-century compositions surviving in later manuscripts; the year 1250 is a midpoint placeholder, not a date of composition. Corrected from a commonly cited range of 1200 to 1400, which conflates composition with the date of the Flateyjarbok copy.
stops.campa: Two hundred years after the voyage, Icelanders write it down. Groenlendinga saga and Eiriks saga rauda are both thirteenth-century compositions working from oral tradition, and they disagree about the discovery, the route, who names what, who is whose sister, and whether Tyrker exists at all. They are literature about history, made on the same island and in the same generation that produces Snorri Sturluson and the saga of Burnt Njal, and by the same method: a family remembered until the family is a story.
suggested_refs: Hauksbok and Skalholtsbok, the two manuscripts of Eiriks saga rauda

stops.name: Flateyjarbok: the Greenlanders' saga survives as an interruption
stops.date_confidence: attested: Groenlendinga saga survives only within Flateyjarbok, compiled 1387 to 1394, where it appears as two separate episodes interpolated into the Saga of Olaf Tryggvason rather than as a standalone text.
stops.campa: Groenlendinga saga has no manuscript of its own. It survives inside Flateyjarbok, the great illuminated codex compiled between 1387 and 1394, cut in two and inserted into the Saga of Olaf Tryggvason as though the discovery of a continent were an anecdote about a Norwegian king. The version with Bjarni Herjolfsson in it, the version with Tyrker and the horse-fall and Freydis with the axe, exists because a fourteenth-century scribe thought it made good filler between chapters of a royal life.
suggested_refs: Flateyjarbok, Stofnun Arna Magnussonar, Reykjavik

stops.name: Ultima Thule: Columbus among the old men of Iceland
stops.date_confidence: attested through Columbus's own note as quoted by his son Ferdinand; what the old men in the harbours said is reported at second hand and cannot be checked. Coordinate inherited byte-for-byte from the existing Thule stop in columbus.journey.json.
stops.campa: In February a Bristol trader carries a Genoese sailor past Iceland and a hundred leagues beyond, into a sea he reports as unfrozen with mighty tides. In the harbours there, old men still talk about lands to the west where their grandfathers' ships once traded: Greenland, and past Greenland. Christopher Columbus writes down the tides and the distances and says nothing about the old men's lands. Four hundred and seventy-six years after Leif's crossing, the memory is still circulating in the same harbours as gossip.
stops.quote: In the month of February, 1477, I sailed a hundred leagues beyond the island of Tile... And to this island, which is as big as England, the English come with their wares, especially from Bristol.
stops.quote_source: Columbus's note, quoted in Ferdinand Columbus, Historie, ch. 4
suggested_refs: Ferdinand Columbus, Historie, ch. 4, the Thule voyage

stops.name: London: the sagas enter English
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the place. The common claim that Beamish gave the first English translation is overstated: his book summarizes Carl Christian Rafn's Antiquitates Americanae of 1837, and Joshua Toulmin Smith published a nearly identically titled English volume in 1839.
stops.campa: North Ludlow Beamish publishes The Discovery of America by the Northmen, in the Tenth Century in London, a rendering of Carl Christian Rafn's Antiquitates Americanae of 1837, and Leif Erikson arrives in English. Joshua Toulmin Smith has beaten him to it by two years with nearly the same title. Arthur Middleton Reeves will produce the translation that fixes the story for a century, The Finding of Wineland the Good, in 1890, and die in a railway accident the year after it appears.
suggested_refs: Carl Christian Rafn, Antiquitates Americanae (Copenhagen, 1837), source of the whole Anglophone tradition

stops.name: Commonwealth Avenue, Boston: a bronze raised on a wrong theory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the statue, the sculptor, and the year; the exact dedication day is not established here. Horsford's Vinland-on-the-Charles thesis is unsupported by any archaeology then or since.
stops.campa: Eben Norton Horsford, chemist and inventor of a baking powder, is certain that Norsemen settled the Charles River and that Vinland was Cambridge, Massachusetts. He is wrong, and he is rich, and he pays for a statue. Anne Whitney casts Leif in bronze in a helmet no Norseman wore, one hand shading his eyes toward a landfall on Commonwealth Avenue. A second casting goes to Juneau Park in Milwaukee the same year. Nothing under the Charles has ever supported him, and the monuments precede the archaeology by seventy-three years.
suggested_refs: Anne Whitney, 'Leif, the Discoverer' (1887), Boston and Milwaukee castings

stops.name: Skolavorduholt, Reykjavik: a gift for a thousand years of law
stops.date_confidence: attested: gifted by the United States in 1930 for the Althing millennium, set on its pedestal 2 May 1932 and unveiled 17 July 1932. The common description placing it before Hallgrimskirkja in 1930 is anachronistic; the church was begun in 1945.
stops.campa: The United States sends Iceland a statue for the thousandth anniversary of the Althing, Alexander Stirling Calder's Leif in a cloak with a longship prow at his feet. Gifted in 1930, it is not set on its pedestal on the hill of Skolavorduholt until 1932. It stands alone on the bare hill for thirteen years. Hallgrimskirkja is begun in 1945 and finished in 1986, rising behind the statue that was there first, which is why every photograph makes the church look like the reason for the man.
suggested_refs: Alexander Stirling Calder's Leif Erikson on Skolavorduholt, Reykjavik

stops.name: L'Anse aux Meadows: George Decker points at the mounds
stops.date_confidence: attested: Helge Ingstad was guided to the site by the local resident George Decker in 1960, and seven seasons of excavation with Anne Stine Ingstad followed through 1968, uncovering eight and possibly nine Norse-style buildings.
stops.campa: George Decker, who lives at L'Anse aux Meadows, takes a Norwegian visitor to see some grassy bumps near the shore that everyone local has always known about. Helge Ingstad has been coasting Newfoundland looking for exactly this. Seven seasons of digging with his wife Anne Stine Ingstad, an archaeologist, turn the bumps into eight Norse buildings, a smithy with bog iron slag, a ring-headed cloak pin, a soapstone spindle whorl. It is a Norse settlement in North America, and it is the only one.
suggested_refs: The Ingstad excavation archive, L'Anse aux Meadows, 1961-1968

stops.name: Washington: October the ninth by proclamation
stops.date_confidence: attested that Wisconsin established the observance in 1929 and that federal proclamation authority dates from 1964; the exact 1964 statute date is not fixed here.
stops.campa: Wisconsin fixes October the ninth as Leif Erikson Day in 1929, and in 1964 Congress authorizes the President to proclaim it; every president since has done so. It is not a public holiday and nobody gets the day off. The date has nothing to do with Leif, whose birth year is a guess and whose death year is unknown. It falls three days before Columbus Day, which is the point of it: a Scandinavian-American answer to an Italian-American one, argued out in the calendar rather than in the ground.
suggested_refs: Wisconsin's 1929 Leif Erikson Day legislation and the federal proclamation tradition from 1964

stops.name: New Haven: a map made to be believed
stops.date_confidence: attested: the map surfaced in 1957 and was unveiled by Yale on 11 October 1965, the day before Columbus Day. McCrone's titanium dioxide analysis is 1972. Yale held a symposium calling it a forgery in 2018, and issued its formal announcement on 1 September 2021.
stops.campa: Yale unveils a parchment map showing Vinlanda Insula west of Greenland and dates it to the 1440s, publishing on the eleventh of October 1965, the day before Columbus Day. The timing is not accidental. In 1972 Walter McCrone finds anatase, a titanium dioxide pigment manufactured from the 1920s, in the ink. Yale calls it a modern forgery at a symposium in 2018 and says so formally in 2021. The map was never needed. The dig at L'Anse aux Meadows had settled the question five years before the unveiling.
suggested_refs: R. A. Skelton and George Painter, The Vinland Map and the Tartar Relation (1965)

stops.name: L'Anse aux Meadows: the year 1021, exactly
stops.date_confidence: attested by the 2021 Nature study, which used the carbon-14 signature of the 993 CE solar storm to date felled wood at the site to 1021. Whether the camp is the saga's Leifsbudir remains disputed; no artifact names Leif.
stops.campa: A solar storm in the year 993 put a spike of carbon-14 into every tree alive on earth. Researchers find the spike in three pieces of wood cut at L'Anse aux Meadows, count the rings outward from it to the bark, and get the same answer three times over: felled in 1021, with metal tools, by people who had not been there before. It is the only precisely dated European presence in the Americas before Columbus. Whether the camp is Leif's Leifsbudir is unproven, and nothing dug there names him.
suggested_refs: Kuitems et al., Nature (2021), 'Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021'
